channel.description: Speedups, and the classical work that keeps taking them back. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Quantum algorithms preset. 5 pay dirt · 3 worth a look.

item.title: Quantum optimization beyond qubit count by low-energy subspace sampling
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent reaches an approximation ratio above 0.95 on a 10000-variable HUBO instance using 100 circuit executions on up to 152 qubits of an IBM processor.

Grade 0.403 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Mateo Alonso, Gonzalo Blázquez-Gil, Pablo Díez-Valle

Figure

Approximation ratio versus algorithm iterations for a 10000-variable heavy-hex HUBO instance on IBM hardware and classical simulation, showing convergence above 0.95 within 100 iterations.

Asks

How can quantum optimization algorithms be scaled to practical problem sizes far exceeding available qubit counts without losing the problem's global structure?

Before

Hardware demonstrations of standard quantum optimization algorithms remained limited to a few hundred variables, or required variational optimization and amplitude estimation.

But

Still fails to match the solution quality of simulated annealing; subproblems can lose hardware-native bipartition when non-adjacent variables are frozen; evaluated on at most 10000 variables and 152 physical qubits.

Tools

Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent (QSSD) · fixed-angle QAOA sampler · IBM Heron and Nighthawk processors · bitflip local search

Abstract

On current digital quantum devices, standard one-qubit-per-variable encodings restrict quantum optimization algorithms to problem sizes where classical solvers typically excel. To avoid this constraint, we introduce Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent (QSSD), an iterative heuristic that decouples the number of problem variables from qubit count, while preserving knowledge of the problem's global structure. QSSD drives the energy descent using a fixed-angle Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm as a low-energy sampler. As the angles are precomputed, each iteration requires just a single circuit execution. We test QSSD on IBM Heron and Nighthawk quantum devices with up to 152 qubits on instances of higher-order unconstrained binary optimization and Max-cut problems. On the largest instance with 10000 variables, QSSD reaches an approximation ratio above 0.95 with 100 circuit executions. We provide both exact and heuristic classical baselines, namely greedy, branch-and-bound solver, and simulated annealing. While our approach still does not match the performance of the best classical baseline, it shows promise in a slower runtime scaling with problem size given a fixed budget. This suggests a regime of large problems where subspace sampling on quantum devices could become competitive, as we also demonstrate how improvements in hardware will lead to better algorithm performance. QSSD is thus a practical heuristic for combinatorial optimization problems that helps bring quantum optimization a step closer to utility.

item.title: Optimal Trace Distance Estimation
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Trace distance between two unknown d-dimensional quantum states can be estimated to additive error ε with Θ(d2ε2log2⁡(d)max⁡{1,ε2log2⁡(d)}) copies of each state.

Grade 0.393 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “sampling-based quantum advantage and its classical spoofing” · Ziyun Chen, Minbo Gao, Qisheng Wang

Asks

Can we estimate the trace distance between two unknown quantum states with fewer samples than standard quantum state tomography?

Before

Full state tomography took O(d2/ε2) samples (O'Donnell and Wright 2016; Haah et al. 2016), while matching lower bound was Ω(d2ε2log2⁡(d)max⁡{1,ε2log2⁡(d)}) (Wang 2026).

But

Both states are arbitrary unknown density operators in dimension d; optimal up to constant factor; sample complexity holds in worst-case full-rank scenario.

Tools

quantum state tomography · Chebyshev polynomial approximation · multiscale polynomial filters · quantum U-statistics · quantum Fourier analysis

Abstract

We present a trace distance estimator with optimal sample complexity. Specifically, the trace distance between two unknown d-dimensional quantum states can be estimated to within additive error ε using \[ Θ(fracd²ε^2log^2(d)max1,ε^2log^2(d)) \] samples of each quantum state. This matches the lower bound of Wang (2026). The estimator combines tomography and polynomial approximation, with variance bounds from quantum Fourier analysis.

item.title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Proposes DOE target deployment of initial fault-tolerant quantum computers by 2028 with ≥100 logical qubits performing 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations, scaling to 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits and 109 to 1010 operations in the 2030s.

Grade 0.377 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond” · Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz, Mallikarjun Shankar, Nicholas Wright

Asks

What strategic milestones, infrastructure readiness, and R&D directions must the DOE pursue to deploy fault-tolerant quantum computers for scientific utility by 2028 and scale into the 2030s?

But

Strategic blueprint and policy proposal; contingent on commercial quantum hardware delivering logical error rates below threshold and sustained national lab infrastructure investment.

Tools

fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) roadmap · systems integration strategy · high-performance computing (HPC) co-design

Abstract

Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.

item.title: Theory-Informed Quantum Error Mitigation for Shor Order Finding with Fourier Neural Operators
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Exact order recovery in Shor order finding rises from 19% to 34% (median Jensen-Shannon divergence falls from 0.64 to 0.32) across 1,351 simulated test cases, and from 35 to 53 correct estimates across 101 hardware circuits on five IBM quantum processors.

Grade 0.374 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Stefano Markidis, Qingxin Yang, Erik Åsgrim, Ivy Peng

Figure

Panels show exact-order recovery, top-3 recovery, and mean Jensen-Shannon divergence across three groups of IBM quantum hardware runs (101 and 35 circuit configurations), comparing raw measurements against the zero-shot transferred Fourier neural operator mitigation.

Asks

Can algorithm-level error propagation models and Fourier neural operators reconstruct ideal output probability distributions and recover hidden periods from noisy quantum circuit executions?

Before

Unmitigated (raw) decoding achieved 19% exact recovery on the simulated test set and 35/101 correct orders on IBM quantum hardware.

But

Evaluated on modular exponentiation with moduli up to N=55 and Mersenne rotation circuits; candidate scoring requires exhaustive or shortlisted candidate evaluation with 𝒪(Qlog⁡Q+RQ) classical complexity per circuit instance.

Tools

Fourier neural operator (FNO) · Fast Fourier transform (FFT) · IBM quantum processors · Shor order finding algorithm

Abstract

Quantum noise distorts the distribution of circuit measurement outcomes, often leaving enough information to infer the algorithm's correct result. To recover this latent information from the noisy distribution in Shor order finding, we introduce a theory-informed quantum error mitigation method. We model how circuit errors shift, broaden, or weaken peaks in the output distribution. These models guide both the generation of synthetic training data and the design of a Fourier neural operator with a learned gain that attenuates or amplifies higher retained Fourier modes. We score each candidate order by averaging the correlations between its ideal distribution and the distributions measured in three circuit executions. The network adjusts these scores to guide the order estimate and determine the weights of a normalized mixture of the ideal distributions. On 1,351 simulated test cases for general modular exponentiation, held out by circuit configuration, exact order recovery rises from 19% to 34%, and the median Jensen-Shannon divergence from the ideal distribution falls by 50%, from 0.64 to 0.32. On 101 Mersenne rotation circuits executed across five IBM quantum processors, a separate model trained and calibrated in simulation increases the number of correct order estimates from 35 to 53. Algorithmic structure can remain recoverable even when noise makes it barely visible.

item.title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Residual learning with exact Frobenius-norm convex projection onto valid density matrices estimates ground-state energy as -0.134 MeV (ideal -0.135 MeV, fidelity 0.999) for a 3-qubit Λ-deuteron model, and -3.014 MeV and -3.045 MeV (fidelities 0.995 and 0.998) for 4-qubit Λ-α potentials.

Grade 0.372 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond” · Sumit Choudhary, Tarunpreet Kaur, Harjeet Kaur, Harpreet Singh

Figure

Ground-state energy in MeV (top) and quantum state fidelity (bottom) versus training-set size N for the 3-qubit system. Proposed ML-QEM (blue) converges stably to the exact energy and unity fidelity, whereas conventional ML-QEM (red) drops below the ground-state energy.

Asks

Can residual learning combined with convex projection to physical density matrices improve machine learning-based quantum error mitigation for hypernuclear ground-state simulations?

Before

Unmitigated hardware estimates deviated substantially, and conventional ML-QEM predicted unphysical energies below exact ground-state values (e.g. -3.822 MeV and -3.739 MeV for 4-qubit potentials).

But

Evaluated on 3-qubit and 4-qubit mapped Hamiltonians; required 1600 VQE-ansatz training states, whereas Haar-random training states failed to recover target ground states.

Tools

Residual ML regression (ridge and RBF kernel ridge) · Frobenius-norm convex projection onto density matrices · IBM Quantum hardware · Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)

Code. https://zenodo.org/records/23969830

Abstract

Noise in quantum devices remains a major challenge for reliable quantum simulations, making quantum error mitigation an important tool for improving their accuracy. Machine learning-based quantum error mitigation (ML-QEM) provides a useful approach, but its performance depends on the training datasets and may produce reconstructed quantum states that are not physically valid. In this work, we introduce an ML-QEM framework that uses residual learning with convex projection to ensure that reconstructed density matrices satisfy physically valid density matrices. We study the effect of different training datasets and regression models using Haar-random and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) ansatz states. We compare the proposed approach with conventional ML-QEM, readout error mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation. The method is tested on IBM quantum hardware for three- and four-qubit simulations of the bound Λ-deuteron and Λ-α hypernuclear systems, respectively. For the three-qubit system, ridge regression trained on VQE-ansatz states gives a ground-state energy of -0.134 MeV, close to the ideal value of -0.135 MeV, with a state fidelity of 0.999. For four-qubit system, kernel ridge regression gives ground-state energies of -3.014 and -3.045 MeV, with corresponding state fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998. These results show that physically constrained reconstruction, along with the choice of training datasets and regression models, can improve ML-QEM performance for the quantum simulations studied in this work.

item.title: A machine learning architecture for scaling of holographic quantum circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Decomposing holographic quantum circuit scaling into syntax generation by a fine-tuned LLM and continuous gate angles via an LSTM produces an 11-qubit generalized W state matching analytical distributions with a total-variation distance of 1.3×10−2.

Grade 0.364 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization” · Cliff Sun, Michael L. Wall

Figure

Relative probability distribution across basis states for an 11-qubit generalized W state comparing analytical values to the hybrid ML pipeline output using 105 simulator shots.

Asks

Can machine learning extrapolate both the discrete circuit syntax and the continuous parameters of holographic quantum circuits to larger system sizes than those seen during training?

But

Demonstrated only on standard and generalized W-state families on up to 15 qubits; restricted to 2-qubit operations (one physical, one ancilla qubit) in classical simulation with 105 shots.

Tools

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) · Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct with 4-bit LoRA · openQASM · Qiskit Aer Simulator

Abstract

We describe an architecture and workflow for learning and generalizing the syntax and parameters of holographic quantum circuits (HQCs), which are natural quantum circuit analogs of classical tensor networks. An HQC uses mid-circuit measurements and resets on a small subset of "physical" qubits whose measurement outcomes become correlated through coupling with a register of persistent "ancilla" qubits, analogous to the physical and bond indices of a tensor network. Hence, an HQC with fixed qubit resources can efficiently generate samples from a large quantum state, and adding qubits to the HQC ansatz has the effect of exponentially increasing the effective bond dimension. Our machine learning approach provides mechanisms for harnessing both features of HQCs by extrapolating the syntax (e.g., a sequence of gates, measurements, and resets) and parameters (e.g., the angles appearing in single-qubit rotations) from a dataset of HQCs to longer or more expressive HQCs. We demonstrate the methodology and its performance on an analytically solvable dataset formed by a vector-valued generalization of the W-state. Finally, we provide an outlook for usage of the methodology for scaling the effective bond dimensions of HQCs in quantum simulation.

item.title: Classical sampling of verifiable graph-state quantum advantage experiments
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Two verifiable graph-state quantum advantage instances on IBM hardware are sampled classically on eight GPUs faster and with higher fidelity than hardware: exact ideal sampling for 70-qubit RGS70, and certified fidelity at least 0.908 for 64-qubit DCS64 with 314 T gates (versus 0.349 on hardware).

Grade 0.358 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Zhongpu Qiu, Yuqi Qing, Jielan Li, Hongxia Hao

Figure

Distribution of scaled output probabilities z=2np(x) for classical GPU samples and quantum hardware samples on RGS70 and DCS64 against ideal and noisy Porter-Thomas distributions.

Asks

Does the check structure required to verify quantum advantage in graph-state experiments fundamentally limit how classically hard the circuits can be?

Before

Hardware reported certified fidelity of at least 0.349 in 870 s for DCS64, and estimated classical sampling times up to 1025 s for RGS70.

But

Sampling cost depends on early axis rank and early Clifford entanglement rather than total T gate count; trade-off between checks and hardness holds conditionally once depth allows checks to cover the early region.

Tools

tensor-network contraction · rank-width methods for graph states · T-gate injection gadgetization · uniform-prefix sampling · 8-GPU cluster

Abstract

Quantum computers are expected to outperform classical ones on some tasks, but a convincing demonstration must be both hard to reproduce classically and verifiable. A recent proposal achieves verifiability by preparing graph states with built-in error detection, so that the quality of the experiment can be certified without simulating it; hardness is added by measuring in a non-Clifford basis or by inserting T gates. We show that the two instances posted to demonstrate this proposal on IBM hardware can be sampled classically on eight graphics processing units, with higher quality than the hardware in comparable or shorter time. For the 70-qubit instance our samples are drawn from the ideal output distribution; for the 64-qubit instance with 314 T gates they come with a certified fidelity of at least 0.908, against 0.349 for the hardware. The reason lies in verification itself: T gates can only be placed where the error detection cannot see them, which pushes them towards the end of the circuit, where they add little classical cost. Our results identify the features that future verifiable advantage experiments must control.

item.title: Classical algorithms for sparse random Hamiltonians via free probability
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Classical algorithm evaluates spectral fluctuations, partition functions, thermal values, and TOC/OTOC correlation functions to error ε in (1/ε)2+o(1) time for sparse random Pauli Hamiltonians.

Grade 0.356 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Matthew Ding, Robbie King, Thomas Schuster

Figure

Exact values versus classical algorithm predictions as free-cumulant truncation order ℓ increases from 2 to 12 for the spectral amplitude, partition function, TOC, and OTOC on an instance with m=80,n=18.

Asks

Can quantum computers yield generic, scalable advantages when simulating quantum many-body systems in traditionally complex, average-case regimes?

Before

Existing classical methods required exponential time due to sign problems and entanglement growth at late evolution times and low temperatures.

But

Applies to fully non-local sparse Pauli Hamiltonians, subexponential precision ε=1/2o(n/log⁡n), and evolution times and inverse temperatures scaling up to 𝒪(n/log⁡n).

Tools

free probability theory · free cumulants · diagrammatic resummation · commutation graph statistics · hypercontractivity

Abstract

The search for quantum advantage in average-case problems is a pressing open question in physics and computer science. The widest conjectured example of such an advantage is in simulation of quantum many-body systems, where sign problems and entanglement growth cause the breakdown of many classical methods. Nonetheless, theoretical evidence for or against such an advantage remains scarce. Here, we investigate this in sparse random non-local Hamiltonians. We design a classical algorithm for such Hamiltonians that enables accurate computation of spectral fluctuations, thermal values, and time-ordered and out-of-time-order correlation functions. For any subexponential precision ε, our algorithm runs in time (1/ε)^(2+o(1)), nearly identical to a quantum simulation. Crucially, this applies even at late evolution times, low temperatures, and near critical points, where existing classical methods require exponential time. Rather than directly simulating a quantum state or operator, our algorithm first computes the model's mean behavior and then a short hierarchy of instance-dependent corrections. These corrections predict long-time behavior based on short-time data using free probability theory.
